logline: Called to a seemingly impossible locked-room death in an old manor, a forensic-minded private detective picks apart small mechanical clues and human lies to expose a sibling's staged murder and the quiet, ingenious trick that made a room appear sealed from within.

entities.sketch: The narrator and private detective, late thirties, forensic-minded, wry, methodical. Hired to consult on the locked-room case.
Local police inspector, by-the-book, keen to close the case quickly, respectful but uneasy about Crowe's methods.
The victim. A sixty-year-old wealthy recluse, owner of Harrow Manor, obsessive about clocks and order, estranged from her only brother.
Lena's younger brother and heir apparent, polished, impatient for control of the estate, with a public quarrel with Lena over money.
Housekeeper of Harrow Manor for decades, fiercely loyal to Lena, guarded about the house's eccentricities and its secrets.
Gardener and odd-job man at the manor, physically capable, quiet, knows the walls and window-sills better than anyone; had a recent argument about pay with Lena.
The old brick manor on a windswept hill; many rooms, service passages, and an overlarge central library that held Lena's clocks and papers.

The locked-room: a ground-floor library within Harrow Manor with one exterior window (heavy latch), a heavy oak door that was bolted from the inside, a mantel with mantle clock, and a desk where Lena's body was found.
An ornate mantel clock on the library fireplace; its hands were stopped at the moment the investigators estimate the fatal wound was inflicted.
A heavy brass letter opener from Lena's desk, found embedded in her chest but with none of the obvious prints and with an oil smear on its haft.
A small linen handkerchief with a monogram; found clutched in Lena's hand. The monogram does not match her own.
An improvised pulley anchor and short length of cord attached to the outer window sill and hidden in the ivy — a possible device for manipulating the window latch or a line from outside.
Lena's folio: a ledger of household accounts and a private notebook in which she annotated names and times. A page is torn out and missing.
A kitchen-style ashtray found on the library sill with cigar ash; one cigar brand was favoured by Henry Harrow.

worldRules: No supernatural explanations; every effect has a physical or human cause.
Physical actions (mechanical triggers, pulleys, climbs) must obey normal physics and the constraints of a late-20th/early-21st-century English manor house.

Forensic facts (stoppage of clock, blood spatter, fingerprints, cigar ash, monogram identification) are admissible and treated realistically — i.e., they can be partial and ambiguous but cannot be ignored without reason.
The narrator (Crowe) is fallible and does not have knowledge beyond what can be reasonably observed, deduced, or learned by questioning witnesses and examining physical evidence.

scenes.intent: Open on the locked-room: establish atmosphere, the impossible seal, and the key physical clues (stopped mantel clock, letter-opener in victim, handkerchief with odd monogram, and the secret pulley on the sill). Set up tension between the inspector who wants a tidy case and the narrator who notices misfits in the evidence.

Interview the household: establish motives and alibis through tight, revealing exchanges with Henry, Mary and Oliver. Crowe inventories the folio and notices a missing page and a fresh oil smear by the sill; Milne grows impatient. Introduce the ashtray and the argument over the folio's contents.

Crowe experiments at night with the clock and the pulley: he reconstructs how a mechanism or outside operator could have stabbed the victim and resealed the room, testing physics and timing. Tension rises when someone notices him on the sill — a near-violent interruption that proves someone wanted the truth concealed.

The reveal: Crowe stages a demonstration for Milne and the household to expose the method and the murderer. Logical deductions from the folio, the monogram, ash, and the pulley point to Henry; a final confrontation forces a confession and explains motive and method, with Milne and the household watching.
